title: Care and Maintenance of Fabrics
summary: Stains, dust, grease and perspiration left on clothes let bacteria and fungus grow (skin problems), make clothes smell, weaken the fabric and spoil the look. Clothes need not be washed every time they are worn. Shaking removes loose dust; brushing with a soft brush in the direction of the pile is for velvet, corduroy, blankets, suits and coats; airing, outdoors in the sun or a ventilated room, dries clothes and removes bad odour. Laundering has three steps: washing or dry cleaning, finishing (starch, gum, brightening agents, drying, ironing, folding) and storing. Washing removes dirt with soap or detergent and water (colourfast fabrics); dry cleaning uses grease absorbents and solvents (leather, fur, selected silks and woollens, zari and costly fabrics).

Collect clothes and supplies at one place; mend tears first (a stitch in time saves nine); sort by fabric, colour, size and weight, amount of dirt, use, soaking time and detergent needed so that colours do not bleed; wash dusters, kitchen cloths and undergarments separately; read care labels.

A stain is an unwanted mark or discolouration caused by contact with another substance. Remove it as soon as possible, before washing, because soap, detergent, hot water and ironing can fix it. Identify a stain by colour (curry yellow, tea or coffee brown, grass green), smell (egg, paint, shoe polish) and feel (paint and sugar make fabric stiff; lipstick and shoe polish make it slippery). Classes: vegetable (tea, coffee, fruit), grease (butter, ghee, oil, curry, shoe polish, tar, oil paint), animal (blood, milk, egg), mineral (rust) and miscellaneous (dye, ink, mildew, grass, perspiration). Techniques: sponging on the wrong side over a blotter, from the outer edge inwards with light circular strokes; dipping the whole fabric for many or large stains.

Treatment: vegetable stains – borax (fresh: boiling water or warm borax solution; old: glycerine, or borax with boiling water). Animal stains (blood, milk, egg) – cold water and soap; avoid heat because the protein sets; old ones in salt water or diluted ammonia. Grease stains – absorbents like chalk or talcum first, then hot water and soap (cotton); paint, shoe polish, nail polish, lipstick, ball pen – sponge with methylated spirit, kerosene or turpentine. Rust – lime juice and salt; old: dilute oxalic acid neutralised with dilute borax. Grass – soap and water, old with methylated spirit; paan – paste of onion in sunlight; ink – soap and cold water, old: sour buttermilk (lassi), lime juice and salt, or bleach. Coloured fabrics are dried in shade. Precautions: act while fresh, test the chemical on a hidden portion, use dilute and mild reagents, rinse several times.

Soaking loosens non-greasy dirt; soak only up to half an hour, not too many clothes together, very dirty clothes separately; do not soak fabrics that weaken when wet (silk, wool) or coloured cottons that bleed. Washing: friction (hand, brush, beating stick) for strong fabrics like cotton and linen; kneading and squeezing for delicate silk, wool and rayon; machine (automatic, semi-automatic, non-automatic). Rinse at least three times until the water is clear. Finishing agents: starch (arrowroot) for cotton, gum arabic for silk, blue or optical brighteners for whiteness. Starch: 2 tablespoons in 5 litres of water suffice for 4–5 clothes; turn the garment inside out, dip in water, wring, dip in starch, squeeze and dry in the sun; do not starch undergarments or close-fitting blouses. Drying: preferably in fresh air and sun, coloured clothes inside out and in shade, undergarments in the sun; long exposure to sun weakens and yellows fabric. Ironing: sleeves, collars and laces first, embroidery from the wrong side, along the length; temperature chart – warm 150 degrees C for wool, silk, polyester, nylon; hot 180 degrees C for cotton and rayon; extra hot 200 degrees C for cotton and linen. Store only completely dry clothes; moist clothes grow fungus and mildew.

White cottons: soak in warm water, wash, rinse, blue, starch, dry in the sun, iron damp. Coloured cottons: no soaking, mild neutral soap, kneading, starch turned inside out, shade drying. Synthetics: lukewarm or cold water, light rubbing, do not squeeze tightly, dry on a hanger, iron with a warm iron. Silk: lukewarm or cold water, neutral soap, no soaking, gum arabic, shade, iron damp with a warm iron. Wool: draw an outline of knitted garments first, mild alkaline detergent in lukewarm water, kneading and squeezing (no rough handling because wool felts), dry flat in shade on the paper outline, store with naphthalene balls.

vsa: Which four precautions should be adopted while laundering cotton clothes (or removing stains)? Give the first four.

Sort the clothes by colour and dirt; mend tears first; soak only white cottons for not more than half an hour and very dirty ones separately; rinse at least three times; dry in the sun (coloured ones in shade) and store only when completely dry.
April 2026
Write any two bases by which you can identify stains. Give two examples of each.

By colour – curry is yellow, tea or coffee is brown, grass is green. By smell – egg, paint, shoe polish have their own smell. By feel – paint or sugar makes the fabric hard and stiff, lipstick or shoe polish makes it slippery (any two bases).
October 2025
Write any four precautions you will adopt while washing woollens at home.

Draw an outline of the knitted garment on paper; use mild alkaline detergent in lukewarm water; wash by kneading and squeezing, no rubbing or wringing; rinse thoroughly; dry flat in the shade on the outline; store dry with naphthalene balls.
April 2024
List four steps involved in the process of laundering clothes.
Soaking, washing, rinsing, finishing (starching or blueing), drying, ironing and storing (any four).
October 2022
Mention four damages that can occur if clothes are not laundered in time.
Bacteria and fungus grow causing skin problems; clothes smell; the fabric loses strength; stains set and become permanent; clothes look dirty and unattractive.
October 2022
Briefly explain the process of laundering a cotton shirt at home.

Mend and sort the shirt; remove stains; soak white shirt in warm soapy water for up to half an hour; wash collar and cuffs with hand friction and the rest by kneading; rinse three times; apply blue and starch; dry in the sun; iron when evenly damp with a hot iron; store when completely dry.
April 2023
Why should stains be removed before washing?
Some stains become permanent when exposed to the chemicals in soap or detergent, hot water and ironing, and old stains need much more effort and give poor results.
Distinguish between washing and dry cleaning.

Washing removes dirt with soap or detergent and water and suits colourfast fabrics; dry cleaning removes dirt with grease absorbents and solvents and is used for leather, fur, selected silks and woollens, zari and costly fabrics.
How much starch and water are needed to starch 4–5 clothes? How can the stiffness be varied?

Two tablespoons of starch in 5 litres of water are enough for 4–5 clothes. For very stiff fabric dilute the full-strength starch with 2–3 times water; add 4–6 times water for reasonably good stiffness.
sa: Why do you wash cotton clothes in soapy water, rinse and starch them? Write the steps of laundering white cotton clothes (any six).

(1) Sort and mend. (2) Remove stains. (3) Soak white cottons in warm water for up to half an hour. (4) Wash in soap solution – light clothes by kneading, heavy ones with a stick, very dirty parts with hand or brush. (5) Rinse at least three times and add blue. (6) Starch for a smooth, fresh look and dry in the sun; iron when damp; store when completely dry.
Describe the technique of sponging to remove a stain.

Place an absorbent paper or cloth (blotter) under the stain so that the right side of the stain faces it; sponge on the wrong side with a soft cloth dipped in the stain remover; rub gently from the outer edge towards the centre with light circular strokes so that the stain does not spread; change the blotter as soon as it shows the stain; rinse well afterwards.
Suggest the correct procedure for washing a brightly printed silk scarf.

Do not soak; use lukewarm or cold water and a good neutral soap with light pressure; rinse well in cold water; apply gum arabic and dry in the shade; iron with a warm iron when evenly damp (silk stains if water is sprinkled on dry cloth); store on a hanger when completely dry.
la: Which five precautions should be adopted while laundering cotton clothes?

(1) Sort white and coloured clothes; read labels; mend tears first. (2) Remove stains before washing. (3) Soak only white cottons in warm water for not more than half an hour, very dirty clothes separately, not too many together. (4) Wash by hand friction, brush or stick as required and rinse at least three times. (5) Use blue and starch (not on undergarments); dry white clothes in the sun and coloured ones inside out in shade; iron when damp and store only when completely dry.
Which five precautions should be adopted while removing stains from clothes (delicate garments)?

(1) Remove the stain while it is fresh. (2) Identify the stain by colour, smell and feel and choose the right agent. (3) Try the chemical on a hidden portion first. (4) Use dilute and mild reagents. (5) Sponge on the wrong side with a blotter underneath, from outer edge inward, or dip. (6) Avoid heat on protein stains. (7) Rinse several times so the chemical does not damage the fabric.

or: Mahima ruined her coloured synthetic clothes after washing them at home. What five possible mistakes may she have committed?

She may have soaked coloured clothes; used hot water, which makes synthetics wrinkle or melt; used strong detergent or rubbed hard; squeezed them tightly; dried them in strong sun instead of shade; or used a hot iron.

la: Reena spoiled her white cotton clothes while removing stains. What could be five possible reasons?

She may not have identified the stain and used the wrong agent; used a strong reagent that damaged the fabric; used heat on a protein stain so it set; let the stain become old before treating it; did not rinse the chemical out properly; or ironed before the stain was removed.
